line.mid: A puffy parka keeps us warm.
line.hi: A puffy parka traps warm air next to our body.
line.e: A puffy parka keeps us warm.
line.u: The parka's fluffy filling traps still air, and still air slows heat leaving your body.
line.t: Parka: down and synthetic fill trap still air, a poor heat conductor, so far less body heat escapes.

line.mid: A wool hat keeps our head warm.
line.hi: A wool hat stops heat escaping from our head.
line.e: A wool hat keeps our head warm.
line.u: A lot of heat escapes from an uncovered head, so a wool hat makes a big difference.
line.t: Hat: any bare skin sheds heat; covering head and ears cuts that loss sharply.

line.hi: Mittens keep fingers together, so they stay warmer than gloves.
line.u: Mittens keep your fingers together, sharing warmth, so they stay warmer than gloves.
line.t: Mittens: fingers share warmth in one pocket with less surface exposed than gloves.

line.mid: A scarf keeps the cold wind off our neck.
line.hi: A scarf blocks the icy wind from our neck and face.
line.e: A scarf keeps the cold wind off our neck.
line.u: Wind blows warm air away from your skin. That is wind chill. A scarf blocks it.
line.t: Scarf: wind strips the warm air layer off skin (wind chill); a scarf shields neck and face.

line.mid: Snow boots keep our toes warm and dry.
line.hi: Snow boots have thick soles so the cold ice cannot reach our toes.
line.e: Snow boots keep our toes warm and dry.
line.u: Thick soles slow the heat flowing from your feet into the ice.
line.t: Boots: insulated soles slow conduction, the heat flow from feet into the ice.

line.mid: Goggles keep the bright snow out of our eyes.
line.hi: Goggles protect our eyes from sunlight bouncing off the snow.
line.e: Goggles keep the bright snow out of our eyes.
line.u: Snow reflects most of the sunlight, which can burn your eyes. Goggles stop snow blindness.
line.t: Goggles: fresh snow reflects up to 80 percent of UV light, which can burn the eye (snow blindness).

line.lo: A map, so we do not get lost.
line.mid: A map shows us the way across the ice.
line.hi: A map helps us find our way across the sea ice.
line.k: A map, so we do not get lost.
line.e: A map shows us the way across the ice.
line.u: Sea ice drifts and cracks, so explorers check the map and change their route.
line.t: Map: sea ice drifts and cracks open into leads, so routes are checked and re-planned.

line.lo: A lamp for the dark night.
line.mid: A head lamp lights the way at night.
line.hi: A head lamp helps in the long Arctic night.
line.k: A headlamp for the dark night.
line.e: A head lamp lights the way at night.
line.u: A headlamp keeps both hands free. In Arctic winter the Sun can stay down for weeks.
line.t: Headlamp: hands stay free, and north of the Arctic Circle winter brings days when the Sun never rises.

line.mid: A fishing rod, to fish through the ice.
line.hi: A fishing rod, to fish through a hole in the ice.
line.e: A fishing rod, to fish through the ice.
line.u: People in the Arctic have fished through holes in the ice for thousands of years.
line.t: Rod and line: jigging through an ice hole is a traditional Inuit way to catch Arctic char and cod.

line.mid: Hot cocoa to warm us up. Yum!
line.hi: Hot cocoa in a flask stays warm for hours. Yum!
line.e: Hot cocoa to warm us up. Yum!
line.u: A vacuum flask has an empty gap in its walls, so heat cannot escape and the cocoa stays hot.
line.t: Vacuum flask: the empty gap between its walls blocks conduction and convection, so drinks stay hot.

ice.q: The drill shows the sea ice here is 18 cm thick. Rule of thumb for solid ice: 15 cm for one person on foot, 20 cm for a group, 25 cm for a snowmobile. What is safe?
ice.say: Before we step out, a safety check. The drill shows 18 centimetres of ice. The rule of thumb is 15 centimetres for one person on foot, 20 for a group, and 25 for a snowmobile. What is safe here?
o: Nothing: ice is never safe under 50 cm
ice.ok: Right. 18 is more than 15, so one person can walk out, but it is less than 20, so no group and no snowmobile.
ice.hint: Compare 18 with each number in the rule. Which ones is it bigger than?
ice.fact: Lake ice can hold one walker at about 10 cm, but sea ice is salty and full of brine pockets, so Arctic guides want more. Ice strength also changes with temperature, snow cover and currents, so people drill and check again as they go.

finder.q: The fish finder counted fish at four depths. Where should we lower the line to get bites fastest?
finder.ok: Good prediction. Most fish showed at 25 metres, so that is where we drop the bait.
finder.hint: Read the bars: which depth has the biggest count?
finder.good: Line at 25 metres. With eight fish down there, bites should come quickly. Watch the float.
finder.slow: Line at 25 metres now, but your first guess would have been slow fishing. Watch how long the first bite takes.
finder.chipGood: Line: 25 m · 8 fish on the finder
finder.chipSlow: Line: 25 m · checking the fish count
finder.moved: Bites are coming faster now that the line sits in the busiest layer.

seal.q: A ringed seal eats about 60 small Arctic cod a day. How many is that in one week?
seal.ok: Yes: 60 times 7 is 420 cod. And one polar bear eats a seal every few days, so the bear depends on all of those fish.
seal.hint: A week has 7 days. Multiply 60 by 7.
seal.fact: Polar bears eat mostly seals. Seals eat mostly fish such as Arctic cod, so the cod sit at the base of the bear's food chain.

ice.q: Three drill readings: 22 cm, 31 cm and 19 cm. Towing the sled needs at least 25 cm everywhere. Using the thinnest reading, how much more ice would we need?
ice.say: Three drill readings: 22, 31 and 19 centimetres. Towing the sled needs at least 25 centimetres everywhere. Using the thinnest reading, how much more ice would we need?
o: None: the average is over 25 cm
ice.ok: Correct: 25 minus 19 is 6 centimetres. The average does not matter; the thinnest spot is where you break through. We walk out and leave the snowmobile on shore.
ice.hint: Safety depends on the weakest spot, not the average. Subtract the thinnest reading from 25.
ice.fact: Sea ice is weaker than lake ice of the same thickness because it holds pockets of salty brine.

finder.q: The finder logged echoes in 30 seconds at each depth. Which depth gives the most fish per minute, and what is that rate?
finder.ok: Right: 18 echoes in 30 seconds doubles to 36 per minute at 12 metres. That layer is where the bait goes.
finder.hint: Find the biggest count, then turn 30 seconds into a full minute.
finder.good: Line set at 12 metres, the busiest layer. Strike the moment the float dips.
finder.slow: Line set at 12 metres. Your first estimate missed, so watch how long the first strike takes; that is the cost of a poor read.
finder.moved: The strike rate is up now that the line is in the 12 metre layer.

seal.q: A ringed seal eats about 3 kg of fish a day, and an Arctic cod weighs about 50 g. How many cod does one seal eat in 30 days?
seal.ok: Correct: 3 kg is 3000 g, divided by 50 g is 60 cod a day, times 30 is 1800. Multiply that by every seal a polar bear eats.
seal.hint: Change 3 kg to grams first. Then cod per day, then times 30.
seal.fact: Polar bears eat mostly seals, so a bear's food really comes from millions of small fish lower in the web.

u.q: A polar bear needs about 2 kg of seal fat a day. One ringed seal gives it about 20 kg of fat. Roughly how many days does one seal last the bear?
u.say: Here is a food web puzzle. A polar bear needs about 2 kilograms of seal fat a day, and one ringed seal gives it about 20 kilograms. Roughly how many days does one seal last?
u.ok: Right: 20 divided by 2 is 10 days. That is why a bear needs to catch a seal every week or so.
u.hint: Divide the fat in one seal by the fat the bear needs each day.
u.fact: Polar bears hunt seals from the sea ice. When the ice melts early, they can go months with little food.

t.q: The sea ice melts 3 weeks earlier than usual. Ringed seals raise their pups in snow dens on the ice. Which effect would you predict first?
t.say: Make a prediction. The sea ice melts three weeks earlier than usual, and ringed seals raise their pups in snow dens on that ice. Which effect would you expect first?
o: Fewer seal pups survive, so polar bears have less to hunt
Polar bears switch to eating clams
Arctic cod disappear before the seals are affected
Nothing changes because seals can breed on land
t.ok: Good prediction. Seal pups need stable ice, and polar bears need seals, so the shock moves up the food web from the ice to the top predator.
t.hint: Start with the animal that needs the ice directly, then follow the arrow to whoever eats it.
t.fact: Scientists have measured that in years with early ice break-up, ringed seal pup survival drops and polar bears in those regions lose body weight.

u.q: Where do the particles that make the northern lights come from?
u.ok: Right. The solar wind carries charged particles from the Sun, and Earth's magnetic field steers them to the poles.

t.q: What starts the chain of events that makes the aurora?
t.ok: Correct. Earth's magnetic field steers solar wind particles toward the poles, where they make oxygen and nitrogen glow.
t.hint: The source is far away in space.
t.fact: Strong solar storms can push the aurora much farther from the poles.
